title: Vector Product of Vectors
short_intro: The vector product (or cross product) of two vectors yields a third vector whose magnitude is proportional to the product of their magnitudes and the sine of the angle between them. Its direction is perpendicular to the plane containing the constituent vectors, following a right-handed screw convention.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of cross product, geometric interpretation as area of parallelogram and triangle, right-hand rule, scalar components in Cartesian coordinates, unit vectors cross products (i x j = k), condition for collinearity and parallelism.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Lagrange's identity, vector triple product, applications to rotational mechanics including torque, angular momentum, central force motion, and Coriolis force.

prerequisites: Resolution of vectors into Cartesian components

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Direction of Vector Product
bullets: The vector product of two vectors A and B is defined as a vector C = A x B = AB sin(θ)n^, where θ is the smaller angle between A and B (0 ≤ θ ≤ π) and n^ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing A and B.
The direction of n^ is given by the right-hand thumb rule: if fingers curl from vector A to vector B, the outstretched thumb points in the direction of A x B.
The cross product is anticommutative: A x B = -(B x A).

concept_notes.heading: Cartesian Component Form
bullets: In terms of orthogonal unit vectors i^, j^, k^, if A = A<sub>x</sub>i^ + A<sub>y</sub>j^ + A<sub>z</sub>k^ and B = B<sub>x</sub>i^ + B<sub>y</sub>j^ + B<sub>z</sub>k^, the cross product is evaluated using a determinant.

The expanded expression is A x B = (A<sub>y</sub>B<sub>z</sub> - A<sub>z</sub>B<sub>y</sub>)i^ - (A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>z</sub> - A<sub>z</sub>B<sub>x</sub>)j^ + (A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>y</sub> - A<sub>y</sub>B<sub>x</sub>)k^.
Cyclic relations for unit vectors: i^ x j^ = k^, j^ x k^ = i^, k^ x i^ = j^; and self cross products vanish: i^ x i^ = 0.

concept_notes.heading: Geometric Interpretation
bullets: The magnitude of the vector product |A x B| represents the area of the parallelogram formed with vectors A and B as adjacent sides.
The area of a triangle formed by vectors A and B as two adjacent sides is given by (1/2)|A x B|.
If A x B = 0 for non-zero vectors A and B, the vectors are collinear or parallel, indicating θ = 0 or π.

concept_notes.heading: Applications in Mechanics
bullets: Torque (τ) is defined as the cross product of position vector r and force F: τ = r x F.
Angular momentum (L) of a particle is given by L = r x p = r x (mv).
Velocity in a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω about a fixed axis is v = ω x r.

derivations.title: Expansion of Cross Product in Cartesian Coordinates
derivations.conditions: Vectors defined in a right-handed orthogonal Cartesian coordinate system
steps: Write vectors A and B in component form: A = A<sub>x</sub>i^ + A<sub>y</sub>j^ + A<sub>z</sub>k^ and B = B<sub>x</sub>i^ + B<sub>y</sub>j^ + B<sub>z</sub>k^.
Apply distributive property of cross product over addition: A x B = (A<sub>x</sub>i^ + A<sub>y</sub>j^ + A<sub>z</sub>k^) x (B<sub>x</sub>i^ + B<sub>y</sub>j^ + B<sub>z</sub>k^).
Expand terms using cross products of unit vectors (e.g., i^ x i^ = 0, i^ x j^ = k^, j^ x i^ = -k^).
Group coefficients of i^, j^, and k^ to form the determinant structure.
derivations.result: A x B = i^(A<sub>y</sub>B<sub>z</sub> - A<sub>z</sub>B<sub>y</sub>) + j^(A<sub>z</sub>B<sub>x</sub> - A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>z</sub>) + k^(A<sub>x</sub>B<sub>y</sub> - A<sub>y</sub>B<sub>x</sub>)

derivations.title: Lagrange's Identity for Vector Products
derivations.conditions: Any two vectors A and B in 3D Euclidean space
steps: Consider the vector identity involving dot and cross products: |A x B|<sup>2</sup> + (A · B)<sup>2</sup>.
Factor out A<sup>2</sup>B<sup>2</sup> to obtain A<sup>2</sup>B<sup>2</sup>(sin<sup>2</sup>(θ) + cos<sup>2</sup>(θ)).
Simplify using trigonometric identity sin<sup>2</sup>(θ) + cos<sup>2</sup>(θ) = 1.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Right-Hand Rule Orientation Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two vectors A and B originating from a common point, with angle θ between them, and a perpendicular vector A x B pointing upwards according to the right-hand screw rule.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the spatial orientation of the cross product vector relative to the plane of the operands.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual MCQs regarding the direction of torque or magnetic force.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Geometric Area of Parallelogram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parallelogram with sides A and B, height h = B sin(θ), illustrating that the magnitude of the cross product equals base times height.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Establishes the physical equivalence between the cross product magnitude and planar area.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct application questions for calculating triangle or parallelogram areas using coordinate vectors.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torque Vector Representation Experiment/Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A wrench of length r acted upon by force F at an angle, showing the resulting torque vector τ pointing perpendicularly out of the plane of rotation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how rotational effect is maximized when force is perpendicular to the position vector.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core mechanics problems involving rotational equilibrium and axis of rotation.

solved_numericals.question: Find the cross product of two vectors A = 2i^ - 3j^ + k^ and B = i^ + 2j^ - 4k^.
Calculate the area of a triangle whose adjacent sides are represented by vectors A = 3i^ + 4j^ and B = -i^ + 2j^.
solution_steps: Compute the cross product A x B = (3i^ + 4j^) x (-i^ + 2j^).
Using unit vector cross products: 3(2)(i^ x j^) + 4(-1)(j^ x i^) = 6k^ - 4(-k^) = 6k^ + 4k^ = 10k^.
Calculate area of triangle = (1/2) |A x B| = (1/2)(10) = 5 square units.

solved_numericals.question: A force F = (2i^ + 3j^ - k^) N acts at a point whose position vector is r = (i^ - j^ + 2k^) m. Determine the torque acting about the origin.
solution_steps: Use the torque formula: τ = r x F.
Set up the determinant with r = [1, -1, 2] and F = [2, 3, -1].
Combine components to get torque vector.

assumptions_and_limitations: The cross product is exclusively defined in 3-dimensional (and 7-dimensional) Euclidean space; it does not have a standard direct definition for 2D planes except by treating 2D vectors as 3D vectors with zero z-components.
The right-hand convention must be strictly maintained; switching to a left-hand coordinate system inverts the sign of the vector product.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Assuming the vector product is commutative, so A x B = B x A.
common_misconceptions.correct: The vector product is anticommutative: A x B = -(B x A).
common_misconceptions.why: Reversing the order of operands reverses the direction of the right-hand thumb rule.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Believing that the cross product of two non-zero vectors can yield a scalar.
common_misconceptions.correct: The vector product always results in a vector quantity.
common_misconceptions.why: By definition, the cross product includes a perpendicular unit vector n^.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Thinking that |A x B| is simply equal to AB without regard to the angle.
common_misconceptions.correct: |A x B| = AB sin(θ), which equals AB only when the vectors are perpendicular (θ = 90°).
common_misconceptions.why: The sine factor accounts for the projection of one vector perpendicular to the other.

quick_revision: A x B = AB sin(θ)n^ and is perpendicular to both A and B.
Definition of Vector Product: A \times B = AB \sin(\theta) \hat{n}
